The Quiet Science of Reading on Screens

By Jane Reporter

Researchers have spent decades trying to understand how people read long articles on screens. A new line of work suggests that typography, line length, and image placement each play a measurable role in comprehension.

In the latest experiment, volunteers read the same essay set in three different layouts. Readers of the narrow-column version recalled key facts more reliably, while wide columns slowed them down without improving understanding.

Images helped when they illustrated the text directly, but decorative pictures hurt recall. The team also found that lazy-loaded figures made no difference to scores as long as they appeared before the reader reached them.

The authors caution that the results come from a laboratory setting with motivated volunteers. Still, they argue that publishers can apply the findings today by keeping columns narrow, captions honest, and pages free of clutter.

Next, the group plans to study newsletters and read-later apps, where saved articles compete with busy inboxes. They expect the same principles to hold, with attention as the scarcest resource of all.
